title: Tax residency of individuals — s 6(1) ITAA 1936
summary: Australian tax residency of an individual is determined by the four tests in the s 6(1) ITAA 1936 definition of 'resident': ordinary concepts ('resides' — Hafza v DGSS four factors), domicile (domicile in Australia unless permanent place of abode outside), the 183-day presence test (Applegate v FCT), and superannuation fund membership (CSS/PSS). Passing ANY one test makes the person a resident taxed on worldwide income. TR 2023/1 provides the ATO's modern primary test + six-factor framework. DTA tie-breakers resolve dual residency. Subsection coverage: s 6(1) 'resident' definition individual limbs (ordinary concepts, domicile, 183-day, superannuation) all mapped; s 995-1 ITAA 1997 cross-reference noted; corporate and trust residency are separate maps (itaa-1936-company-residency, itaa-1936-trust-residency).

nodes.body: Australian tax residency for individuals is determined by the s 6(1) ITAA 1936 definition of 'resident' — four statutory tests: ordinary concepts ('resides'), domicile, 183-day, and superannuation fund membership. Passing any one test makes the person a resident, taxed on worldwide income. TR 2023/1 now provides the ATO's modern framework for the ordinary concepts test.

nodes.label: ORDINARY CONCEPTS — Does the person 'reside' in Australia?
nodes.body: The leading test. Hafza v DGSS (1985) 6 FCR 444 sets out the four factors: (1) physical presence in Australia; (2) the quality of that presence (habitual or usual place of abode); (3) the person's domicile; and (4) the purpose of the presence and the person's ties to Australia (family, business, assets, social). No single factor is decisive — it is a question of fact and degree. TR 2023/1 now sets out a primary test (residing in Australia — usually indicated by living there) and a six-factor secondary analysis.

nodes.label: DOMICILE TEST — Is the person's domicile in Australia, and do they lack a permanent place of abode outside Australia?
nodes.body: A person whose domicile is in Australia is a resident unless their permanent place of abode is outside Australia (s 6(1)(a)(ii) ITAA 1936). 'Permanent place of abode' is the enduring home — not necessarily the only home, but the fixed, habitual home. Temporary absence does not break it.

nodes.label: 183-DAY TEST — Has the person been physically present in Australia for more than half the income year?
nodes.body: A person actually present in Australia, continuously or intermittently, during more than one-half of the year of income is a resident unless their usual place of abode is outside Australia and they do not intend to take up residence in Australia (s 6(1)(a)(iii) ITAA 1936). The exception requires BOTH elements. Applegate v FCT (1979) is the leading authority on the boundary.

nodes.label: SUPERANNUATION TEST — Is the person a member of CSS, PSS or a related scheme?
nodes.body: A person who is a member of the CSS (Commonwealth Superannuation Scheme), PSS (Public Sector Superannuation Scheme) or a scheme for the benefit of employees of a Commonwealth authority is a resident (s 6(1)(a)(iv) ITAA 1936).

nodes.label: RESIDENT — individual taxed on worldwide income
nodes.body: Once any one test is satisfied, the individual is a resident of Australia for tax purposes: worldwide income assessable (s 6-5 ITAA 1997), worldwide gains subject to CGT, foreign income tax offsets may apply (Div 770 ITAA 1997).

nodes.label: FOREIGN RESIDENT — individual taxed only on Australian-source income
nodes.body: A non-resident individual is taxed only on Australian-source income: employment income for services performed in Australia, dividends/interest/royalties from Australian sources, and capital gains on taxable Australian property (Div 855 ITAA 1997). No tax-free threshold applies.

nodes.label: MODERN FRAMEWORK — TR 2023/1: apply the primary test, then the six-factor analysis
nodes.body: TR 2023/1 (issued December 2023, replaces the old IT 2650 approach) sets out: primary test — does the individual reside in Australia (usually indicated by living in Australia, especially with family/home); if not clear, a six-factor analysis: (1) intention or purpose of presence; (2) family and business/employment ties; (3) maintenance and location of assets; (4) social and living arrangements; (5) physical presence pattern; (6) frequency, regularity and duration of visits. The ruling also addresses temporary residents and the boundary with the statutory tests.

nodes.label: DTA TIE-BREAKER — Is the individual a dual resident under the applicable DTA?
nodes.body: If the individual is a resident under Australian domestic law AND a resident of a treaty partner under its domestic law, the DTA tie-breaker rules (e.g., AU-UK Article 4, AU-US Article 4) resolve the conflict: (1) permanent home available; (2) centre of vital interests; (3) habitual abode; (4) nationality; (5) mutual agreement. The winner is treated as a resident of only that country for treaty purposes.
